items.title: The 2027 COLA Is Coming: How September Inflation Sets Your Social Security Raise
items.body:
Every October, millions of Social Security beneficiaries wait for one number: the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, that will apply to their monthly benefit starting in January. This year, the final piece of that calculation arrives with the September Consumer Price Index (CPI) report. Here is how the formula works, why a raise can feel smaller than it looks, and what to watch next.

*This article is for general information only and is not personal financial advice. Check the Social Security Administration (SSA) announcement for the official 2027 figure.*

## What a COLA actually is

Social Security benefits are tied to inflation by law. The goal of the COLA is simple: keep the purchasing power of benefits from eroding as prices rise. Without it, a benefit that covers a given basket of goods today would cover less each year.

The COLA also applies to Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments, so the same percentage reaches some of the lowest-income beneficiaries in the program.

## The formula, step by step

The adjustment is not based on a single month of data, and it is not based on the headline CPI that makes the news. The process works like this:

1. **The index used is the CPI-W.** That is the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It is related to, but not identical to, the more widely quoted CPI-U.
2. **Only the third quarter counts.** The SSA takes the average CPI-W for July, August and September.
3. **It compares that average with the prior year's third quarter.** If this year's average is higher than last year's, the percentage difference becomes the COLA.
4. **The result is rounded to the nearest tenth of a percent.**
5. **If prices did not rise, there is no increase.** In that case benefits stay the same; they are not reduced.

Because the September report supplies the last of the three monthly readings, the COLA can be calculated and announced as soon as that report is released, typically in mid-October.

## Why the raise can feel smaller than it looks

A headline percentage is only part of the story. Several factors can make a COLA feel modest in practice.

- **Medicare Part B premiums.** For most beneficiaries, the Part B premium is deducted directly from the Social Security check. When the premium rises, it can absorb a meaningful share of the increase. A "hold harmless" rule protects many people from a premium increase that would reduce their net benefit, but it does not apply to everyone, such as people newly enrolled or higher earners who pay income-related amounts.
- **The index may not match your spending.** The CPI-W measures a broad basket of goods and services. Retirees often spend a larger share of their budgets on health care and housing than that basket reflects, so their personal inflation rate can differ from the national figure. Researchers have long debated whether an index designed specifically for older Americans would be more accurate.
- **Inflation is cumulative.** A COLA reflects the past year's price changes. If prices have risen for several years in a row, a single year's adjustment does not reverse the earlier increases in the cost of living.
- **Taxes.** Depending on total income, up to 85 percent of Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax. The income thresholds that trigger this are not indexed to inflation, so a larger share of benefits can become taxable over time.
- **Timing lag.** The adjustment is based on July-to-September data and takes effect in January, which means prices can keep moving in the months in between.

## A quick illustration

Suppose a retiree receives $2,000 a month and the COLA is 2.5 percent. The gross increase would be $50 a month, bringing the benefit to $2,050. If the Medicare Part B premium rises by $15 that month and is deducted from the check, the net gain is closer to $35 before any tax effects. The exact numbers differ for every household, but the arithmetic shows why the gross and net figures can diverge.

## Other numbers that change in January

The COLA announcement usually comes with other updates for the new year. These commonly include:

- **The taxable maximum.** This is the cap on earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax. It typically rises each year with average wage growth.
- **The earnings test thresholds.** People who claim benefits before full retirement age and keep working may have benefits temporarily withheld above certain earnings limits.
- **The quarter-of-coverage amount.** This determines the earnings needed to earn work credits.
- **Medicare premiums and deductibles.** These are announced separately by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, usually in the fall.

## What retirees should watch next

- **The official SSA announcement.** It usually follows the CPI release the same morning and is posted at ssa.gov.
- **Your COLA notice.** The SSA typically sends notices to beneficiaries in December, and many people can see the details in their my Social Security online account.
- **The Medicare Part B premium.** Compare it with your COLA to estimate your net change.
- **Your withholding.** If you have federal income tax withheld from benefits, consider whether the new amount still matches your situation.
- **The program's long-term finances.** The annual Trustees Report projects the funding outlook for the trust funds, which is a separate question from the COLA but one that shapes the wider debate over benefits.

## The bottom line

The 2027 COLA is a mechanical calculation: the average CPI-W for the third quarter compared with the same period a year earlier. The September CPI report completes that calculation. What matters to each household, however, is the net amount after Medicare premiums and taxes, and how it compares with the prices that household actually faces. Once the official figure is announced, reviewing your own budget against the new benefit amount is the most useful next step.

items.title: Medicare Open Enrollment Starts October 15: Original Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage
items.body:
Every fall, millions of Americans with Medicare get a chance to revisit a decision that affects their health care and their budgets for the entire following year. The annual Open Enrollment Period runs from **October 15 to December 7**, and any changes made during that window take effect on **January 1**.

For many people, the central question is whether to stay with Original Medicare or choose a Medicare Advantage plan. Neither option is right for everyone. Here is a plain-English look at what to compare before the deadline.

## What Open Enrollment Lets You Do

During the fall window, people with Medicare can generally:

- Switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan (Part C).
- Switch from a Medicare Advantage plan back to Original Medicare.
- Change from one Medicare Advantage plan to another.
- Join, drop or change a stand-alone Part D prescription drug plan.

If you are already satisfied with your coverage, you do not have to do anything. But plans can change their costs, provider networks, covered drugs and benefits from year to year, so a quick review is worthwhile even if you plan to stay put.

## The Two Basic Paths

### Original Medicare

Original Medicare is run by the federal government and has two main parts: Part A (hospital insurance) and Part B (medical insurance). Key features include:

- **Broad provider access.** You can generally see any doctor or visit any hospital in the country that accepts Medicare.
- **No referrals needed** to see most specialists.
- **Cost sharing without a yearly out-of-pocket cap.** You typically pay a deductible and a share of costs, often 20% of Part B-covered services, and there is no annual limit on what you could owe.
- **Add-ons are separate.** Prescription drug coverage (Part D) and Medigap supplemental policies, which help pay deductibles and coinsurance, are purchased separately and come with their own premiums.

### Medicare Advantage (Part C)

Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurers approved by Medicare. They must cover everything Original Medicare covers, and most bundle in extras. Key features include:

- **A provider network.** Many plans are HMOs or PPOs, which means your costs may be lower, or coverage may apply only, when you use in-network providers.
- **A yearly cap on in-network spending.** Unlike Original Medicare, Advantage plans must set a maximum out-of-pocket limit for covered services.
- **Extras.** Many plans include prescription drug coverage and may add dental, vision, hearing or fitness benefits.
- **Prior authorization.** Some services may require the plan's approval before you receive care.
- **Low or $0 plan premiums are common,** though you generally must keep paying your Part B premium.

## Five Things to Compare

### 1. Your doctors and hospitals

Check whether the physicians, specialists and hospitals you rely on are in a plan's network. Networks can change, so confirm directly with your providers and with the plan rather than relying on last year's information.

### 2. Total cost, not just the premium

A low monthly premium does not tell the whole story. Look at the deductible, copayments, coinsurance and the out-of-pocket maximum. If you have a chronic condition or expect surgery, estimate what a high-use year might cost under each option.

### 3. Prescription drugs

Plans maintain lists of covered drugs, called formularies, and these can change. Enter your current medications into the plan finder tool on Medicare.gov to compare estimated annual costs, and confirm that your pharmacy is in the plan's network. Part D also has an annual limit on out-of-pocket drug spending that adjusts each year, so check the current figure.

### 4. Extra benefits and how you will actually use them

Dental, vision and hearing benefits can be valuable, but they often come with annual dollar limits or restrictions. Ask what is covered, what is capped, and whether the providers you would use participate.

### 5. Travel and flexibility

If you spend part of the year in another state or travel often, check how a plan handles care outside its service area. Original Medicare works nationwide, while many Advantage plans are built around a local region.

## A Timing Issue Worth Knowing About

Switching is not always symmetrical. If you move from Medicare Advantage back to Original Medicare and want a Medigap policy, insurers in most states are allowed to review your health history and may charge more or decline to sell you a policy outside of certain protected periods. People who are considering a move away from Advantage should learn their state's rules before they leave a plan.

Also note that if you are already in a Medicare Advantage plan, there is a separate Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period from January 1 to March 31. It allows one change, either to another Advantage plan or back to Original Medicare, but it does not permit you to join a stand-alone drug plan.

## Where to Get Help

- **Medicare.gov** offers a plan finder tool and the annual "Medicare & You" handbook.
- **1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227)** connects you with Medicare representatives.
- **State Health Insurance Assistance Programs (SHIPs)** provide free, unbiased, one-on-one counseling in every state.

Be cautious with unsolicited calls, mailers and ads. Medicare will not call you out of the blue to sell a plan, and you should never give out your Medicare number to someone you did not contact yourself.

## The Bottom Line

There is no universally better choice between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. The right answer depends on your health needs, your preferred doctors, your budget and how much predictability you want. Reviewing your plan's annual notice of changes, comparing options and confirming details with official sources before December 7 can help you avoid surprises in the new year.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and is not insurance, legal or medical advice. Plan details and costs vary by location and change annually; verify current information with Medicare or a licensed counselor.*

items.title: Beyond the Candidates: How State Ballot Measures Shape Policy in November
items.body:
When Americans head to the polls in November, the biggest names on the ticket will be candidates for the Senate, the House and governor's offices. But look further down the ballot and many voters will find something different: questions that ask them to decide a policy directly. Ballot measures can raise the minimum wage, change how taxes are collected, rewrite election rules or amend a state constitution, and the outcomes often have a more immediate effect on daily life than a single seat in a legislature.

## What Is a Ballot Measure?

A ballot measure is a question put directly to voters rather than to elected officials. Depending on the state, it might be called a proposition, a question, an amendment or a referendum. The wording differs, but the idea is the same: a "yes" or "no" vote can change a law or a state's constitution.

Ballot measures generally fall into a few categories:

- **Initiated statutes:** Citizens propose a new law, gather enough signatures to qualify, and voters approve or reject it.
- **Initiated constitutional amendments:** Citizens propose a change to the state constitution through the same signature process, in states that allow it.
- **Legislative referrals:** The legislature places a proposed law or constitutional amendment on the ballot. In most states, constitutional amendments must go to voters before they take effect.
- **Veto referendums:** Citizens collect signatures to ask voters whether a law the legislature has already passed should stay in effect.

## How Measures Get on the Ballot

The rules vary widely from state to state. Roughly half of the states allow some form of citizen-initiated measure, while every state uses legislative referrals in some form. Where citizen initiatives are allowed, supporters typically must:

1. **File a petition** with a state office, often including the exact text of the proposal.
2. **Receive an official title and summary**, which is the language voters will eventually see. This wording is sometimes the subject of legal disputes.
3. **Collect signatures** from registered voters. The required number is often tied to turnout in a previous election, and some states also require signatures to be spread across regions.
4. **Pass verification**, in which election officials check signatures and the measure may face court review before it is certified.

Because of this process, campaigns often start more than a year before Election Day. Signature drives can be costly, and legal challenges over wording, subject matter or signature validity can decide whether a measure appears on the ballot at all.

## The Issues Voters Are Weighing

Ballot measures tend to cluster around a handful of recurring subjects. Several categories are common in many election cycles.

### Wages and Workplace Rules

Minimum wage proposals have appeared on ballots in many states, along with questions about paid sick leave and tipped-worker pay. Because wage rules affect household budgets and business costs at the same time, these measures draw attention from both employees and employers.

### Taxes and Budgets

Voters are frequently asked to approve or reject changes to property, income or sales taxes, to set limits on government spending, or to authorize bonds for schools, roads and other public projects. These questions often come with detailed fiscal analyses prepared by nonpartisan state agencies.

### Election Rules

Some of the most closely watched measures concern the process of voting itself. Topics have included voter identification requirements, ranked-choice voting, open primaries, redistricting commissions and campaign finance rules. Since these measures set the framework for future elections, they can shape which candidates compete and how votes are counted.

### Other Policy Areas

Housing, health care, public safety, education funding and environmental policy also regularly appear. Individual states may also present highly local questions that never become national news.

## Why These Measures Can Matter as Much as Any Candidate

A single legislator is one vote among many. A ballot measure, by contrast, can become law or a constitutional provision on its own once voters approve it. That has several consequences:

- **Direct and durable change.** A constitutional amendment can be difficult to undo, since reversing it often requires another statewide vote.
- **Policy outside the legislature.** Voters can act on topics that lawmakers have been unwilling or unable to address, or can reject proposals the legislature has passed.
- **Influence on turnout.** High-profile measures can motivate people to vote who might otherwise skip a midterm election.
- **Ripple effects.** Successful measures in one state are often studied and copied by advocates in others.

## How to Prepare as a Voter

Ballot measures can be dense, and the wording is not always easy to follow. A few habits help:

- **Read the full text and the official summary,** not just the title. Official voter guides, usually published by the secretary of state or election office, include the exact language and arguments for and against.
- **Check the fiscal analysis.** Many states publish independent estimates of what a measure would cost or save.
- **Understand what "yes" and "no" mean.** On some measures, a "yes" vote keeps current law while a "no" vote changes it, or the reverse. The wording can be counterintuitive.
- **Look at who is funding each side.** State campaign finance databases list major donors for and against a measure.
- **Use trusted, nonpartisan sources.** Local newsrooms, nonpartisan research organizations and official state publications can help separate the facts from campaign advertising.
- **Make a plan to vote the whole ballot.** Some voters leave ballot questions blank, a practice known as "ballot roll-off." Reviewing a sample ballot ahead of time can make it easier to decide.

## The Bottom Line

Campaign coverage naturally focuses on candidates, but the ballot is often much longer than the headlines suggest. Taking time to learn about the questions that appear on your own ballot is one of the most direct ways to have a say in the rules, taxes and policies that affect your state. Check your local election office for a sample ballot and voter guide, and confirm your registration status and voting options well before Election Day.
